name: Muhammad Danish Khan
title: Backend Developer · Java (Spring Boot) · Node.js
summary: Backend developer with 2+ years of experience building and scaling high-traffic REST APIs in Java (Spring Boot) and Node.js. Strongest in performance work: Redis caching, native SQL tuning and async processing. I cut critical API latency from 900ms+ to ~70ms on Tamasha, a live streaming platform used by millions during peak cricket events, and co-founded Scorka, a live cricket scoring platform I built end to end.

experience.description: Backend developer on Tamasha, Pakistan's leading live streaming platform.
points: Engineered and optimised REST APIs serving 5M+ peak concurrent users during high-traffic events such as India–Pakistan cricket matches.
Cut critical API response times from 900ms+ to ~70ms (~92%) by profiling with JProfiler and JMeter, adding Redis caching and rewriting ORM queries as optimised native SQL.
Integrated RabbitMQ for asynchronous event processing, raising throughput and decoupling core services under peak load.
Delivered backend features across the Trivia, User, Subscription, Content and Live modules, built for high availability and horizontal scalability.
Built and tested REST APIs for internal modules in Java and Spring Boot under senior developer mentorship.
Gained production experience with RabbitMQ, Redis and MySQL, and took part in profiling sessions that found and fixed slow queries.
Built 2D platformer games from scratch in Construct 3, owning the game logic: player mechanics, enemy behaviour, collision systems and level progression.

projects.name: Scorka
projects.description: Most local cricket in Pakistan is still scored on paper, so players have no records, rankings or live scores. Scorka lets anyone score a match ball by ball on their phone, run tournaments and build a player record over time.

sections.title: The problem
sections.body: Local cricket is played every weekend in towns and villages across Pakistan, but it is scored in notebooks. Scores get lost, tournaments are organised over WhatsApp, and a good player has nothing to show for years of matches.

sections.title: What I built
sections.body: I architected and built the backend end to end: 23 JPA entities and 83 REST endpoints across auth, team, tournament, series and match modules, supporting league, round-robin and pool-group formats.
points: Tournaments with teams, fixtures and live points tables.
Player rankings by village and district, built from match data.
Teams, invites, join requests and in-app notifications.

sections.title: Ball-by-ball scoring engine
sections.body: Every ball is stored as an event, and everything else is computed from those events.
points: Handles legal deliveries, extras (wide, no-ball, bye, leg-bye), seven dismissal types, over sequencing and undo-last-ball.
Batting, bowling, fielding and team stats are recomputed from raw ball events into leaderboards.

sections.title: Reliable on bad networks
sections.body: Matches are scored at the ground, where the internet is often weak.
points: Idempotent ball recording keyed on a client-generated event ID, so a retried request never records a ball twice.
A sync queue with retry tracking for offline-first clients.

sections.title: Architecture
sections.body: The Android app (React Native) talks to a Spring Boot API. MySQL reads and writes go through separate datasources, each with its own HikariCP pool, entity manager and transaction manager, tuned for read-heavy scorecard traffic. Redis holds login codes with a TTL.

sections.title: Auth and errors
points: Redis-backed OTP login with TTL, and JWT access and refresh tokens behind a custom auth filter.
45 typed exceptions behind a global error mapper.
OpenAPI-documented endpoints.

sections.title: A security flaw I caught
sections.body: A first design for team join requests stored them in the same table as captain invites. Because invites are accepted by the invited player, a player could have accepted their own request and joined any team. I moved join requests to their own table, let only the captain accept them, and covered every case with tests before release.

sections.title: Quality and shipping
points: 519 automated backend tests.
An independent QA engineer ran 153 test cases on a real device: the scoring maths was verified ball by ball and the app had 0 crashes.
Running in production on a Linux server, with verified Android App Links so shared scorecards open straight in the app.
Released to testers on Google Play.

sections.title: Team
sections.body: I own the backend, database, server and deployment. The mobile app was built with my partner Fahad.

projects.name: Tamasha
projects.tagline: Pakistan's leading live streaming & entertainment platform
projects.description: Tamasha streams shows, movies, live TV and live sports, peaking at 5M+ concurrent users during major cricket events. I work on its backend: REST APIs, the Redis caching layer, RabbitMQ async processing and live streaming.
projects.note: I work on Tamasha as a backend engineer at Mercurial Minds. Its code and internal details are confidential, so this page describes my role only.

sections.title: Where I work
sections.body: The backend is split into modules. I have delivered features across the Trivia, User, Subscription, Content and Live modules, built for high availability and horizontal scalability.

sections.title: 900ms to 70ms
sections.body: Some critical APIs were taking more than 900ms. I profiled them with JProfiler and load-tested them with JMeter, then fixed the causes.
points: Added Redis caching strategies for hot data.
Rewrote slow ORM queries as optimised native SQL.
Resolved N+1 query problems and added the right indexes.
Result: ~70ms, about 92% faster, on a platform that peaks at 5M+ concurrent users.

sections.title: Async processing
points: Integrated RabbitMQ for asynchronous event processing.
Raised throughput and decoupled core services under peak load.

sections.title: Designing new APIs
points: Designed the architecture of new APIs and implemented them end to end.
